type-1.when: Coefficients are given and you need sums or products of roots.
type-1.why: Expanding the factorised polynomial gives the coefficient–root relations.
type-1.mistake: Missing the alternating signs or the leading coefficient.
type-1.hint: Write down the degree and leading coefficient before matching terms.

type-2.when: The new roots are reciprocals of the original roots.
type-2.why: Reciprocal sums and products can be expressed using the original root sums.
type-2.mistake: Using reciprocals when an original root is zero.
type-2.hint: Put the reciprocal sum over a common denominator.

type-3.when: A low power sum is required without solving for the roots.
type-3.why: Expanding a square or cube connects power sums with products of different roots.
type-3.mistake: Confusing a sum of squares with the square of a sum.
type-3.hint: Start with the identity for the square or cube of a sum.

type-4.when: The question asks for higher powers or negative powers of the roots.
type-4.why: Every root satisfies the original polynomial, so adding the substituted equations gives a recurrence.
type-4.mistake: Taking the zeroth power sum to be one instead of the number of roots.
type-4.hint: Substitute one root into the original equation, then multiply by a useful power.

type-5.when: Each new root is a specified expression in an old root.
type-5.why: The substitution makes the transformed roots satisfy the new polynomial.
type-5.mistake: Substituting into only some terms or failing to clear denominators.
type-5.hint: Express the old variable in terms of the new one first.

type-1.when: A reciprocal of a linear expression needs sketching.
type-1.why: The denominator zero and limiting value locate the asymptotes.
type-1.mistake: Drawing the curve through its vertical asymptote.
type-1.hint: Find the denominator zero and check the sign on each side.

type-2.when: Numerator and denominator are both linear.
type-2.why: Division separates a constant from a shifted reciprocal.
type-2.mistake: Using the ratio of constant terms for the horizontal asymptote.
type-2.hint: Rewrite the numerator as a multiple of the denominator plus a remainder.

type-3.when: A constant is divided by a quadratic with two real factors.
type-3.why: Denominator zeros split the branches; a derivative locates stationary points.
type-3.mistake: Assuming the middle branch has the same sign as the outer branches.
type-3.hint: Mark both denominator zeros before finding branch signs.

type-4.when: A linear numerator is divided by two linear factors.
type-4.why: Intercepts, asymptotes and stationary points determine the branch shapes.
type-4.mistake: Treating a numerator zero as an asymptote.
type-4.hint: Find numerator and denominator zeros separately.

type-5.when: A quadratic is divided by a quadratic.
type-5.why: Leading terms give the limit at infinity; zeros and derivatives give the remaining features.
type-5.mistake: Assuming the horizontal asymptote can never be crossed.
type-5.hint: Compare the leading coefficients, then find the intercepts.

type-6.when: The numerator degree is one more than the denominator degree.
type-6.why: Polynomial division leaves a linear term and a remainder that tends to zero.
type-6.mistake: Keeping the remainder as part of the asymptote equation.
type-6.hint: Perform the polynomial division before sketching.

type-7.when: A rational function has no real denominator zeros and its range is required.
type-7.why: A value is in the range only if the equation has a real solution for the input.
type-7.mistake: Including a limiting value without checking whether it is attained.
type-7.hint: Set the function equal to a general value and rearrange in the input variable.

type-8.when: A sketch is transformed using absolute values or a reciprocal.
type-8.why: Absolute values reflect the relevant part; taking a reciprocal exchanges zeros and poles where defined.
type-8.mistake: Reflecting the wrong part of the original graph.
type-8.hint: Identify whether the absolute value is applied to the input or the output.

type-1.when: A sum contains powers of the index.
type-1.why: Summation is linear, so standard sums can be combined term by term.
type-1.mistake: Ignoring a starting index other than one.
type-1.hint: Expand the summand and list the standard sums you need.

type-2.when: Successive terms can be written as differences.
type-2.why: Adjacent terms cancel, leaving only boundary terms.
type-2.hint: Write out the first few and last few differences.

type-3.when: A finite sum is followed by a sum to infinity.
type-3.why: The infinite sum is the limit of the finite expression when that limit exists.
type-3.mistake: Taking a limit without stating the convergence condition.
type-3.hint: Find a finite expression before letting the upper limit increase.

type-1.when: An inverse matrix is requested and the determinant is nonzero.
type-1.why: The adjugate formula produces a matrix whose product with the original is the identity.
type-1.mistake: Forgetting to transpose the cofactor matrix.
type-1.hint: Calculate the determinant before starting the cofactors.

type-2.when: An inverse is to be found using row operations.
type-2.why: Applying the same row operations to the identity records the inverse transformation.
type-2.mistake: Performing a row operation on only half of the augmented matrix.
type-2.hint: Write the matrix and identity side by side.

type-3.when: A matrix represents a geometric transformation.
type-3.why: The images of basis vectors determine the linear transformation.
type-3.mistake: Reading columns as images of rows when using column vectors.
type-3.hint: Apply the matrix to the two standard basis vectors.

type-4.when: Two transformations are combined or one is reversed.
type-4.why: Matrix multiplication composes maps, and an inverse reverses a nonsingular map.
type-4.mistake: Multiplying transformation matrices in the wrong order.
type-4.hint: Write which transformation happens first before multiplying.

type-5.when: Points on a line must be mapped onto that same line.
type-5.why: Requiring every image point to satisfy the line equation gives coefficient conditions.
type-5.mistake: Assuming invariant means every point stays fixed.
type-5.hint: Transform a general point on the line, not just one chosen point.

type-1.when: A perpendicular vector, triangle area or parallelepiped volume is required.
type-1.why: Cross and scalar triple products measure the relevant perpendicular component.
type-1.mistake: Forgetting to halve a parallelogram area for a triangle.
type-1.hint: Choose the two directions that lie in the required plane.

type-2.when: A plane is specified by a normal or by two independent directions.
type-2.why: The displacement between two points in a plane is perpendicular to its normal.
type-2.mistake: Using a direction in the plane as its normal.
type-2.hint: Find a normal, then substitute a known point.

type-3.when: A shortest distance from a point to a line is required.
type-3.why: The cross product isolates the component perpendicular to the line.
type-3.mistake: Forgetting to divide by the direction vector magnitude.
type-3.hint: Choose a point on the line and form the displacement from it.

type-4.when: A point and a Cartesian plane equation are given.
type-4.why: Dividing by the normal magnitude converts the plane expression to perpendicular distance.
type-4.mistake: Omitting the absolute value in a distance.
type-4.hint: Put the plane in a consistent normal form before substituting.

type-5.when: Two non-parallel lines do not intersect.
type-5.why: The shortest joining segment is perpendicular to both line directions.
type-5.mistake: Assuming the two line parameters have the same value.
type-5.hint: Use a separate parameter for a general point on each line.

type-6.when: An acute line–plane or plane–plane angle is requested.
type-6.why: A plane normal is perpendicular to the plane, linking its angle with a line to the complement.
type-6.mistake: Using cosine directly for the line–plane angle.
type-6.hint: Decide whether the angle is between directions or between normals.

type-7.when: Two non-parallel planes meet in a line.
type-7.why: Solving both plane equations leaves one free parameter.
type-7.mistake: Choosing a point that satisfies only one of the planes.
type-7.hint: Leave one coordinate free and solve for the other two.

type-1.when: A transformed hyperbolic graph is to be sketched.
type-1.why: The standard graph carries the stated stretches, reflections and shifts.
type-1.mistake: Reversing the sign of a horizontal translation.

type-2.when: An equation contains sinh, cosh or tanh.
type-2.why: Exponential definitions or standard identities turn it into an algebraic equation.
type-2.mistake: Accepting a tanh value outside its real range.
type-2.hint: Choose an exponential variable or isolate the hyperbolic function.

type-3.when: An inverse hyperbolic value must be written in logarithmic form.
type-3.why: The logarithmic form solves the corresponding exponential equation.
type-3.mistake: Using the logarithmic formula outside its domain.
type-3.hint: Identify the inverse function and its domain before substitution.

type-4.why: Both sides reduce using the exponential definitions and standard identities.
type-4.mistake: Using circular identities with the wrong hyperbolic sign.
type-4.hint: Start from one side and replace the hyperbolic terms by exponentials.

type-1.when: The relation between input and output is implicit.
type-1.why: The chain rule accounts for every occurrence of the dependent variable.
type-1.mistake: Missing a derivative factor when differentiating a term containing the dependent variable.
type-1.hint: Differentiate both sides with respect to the independent variable.

type-2.when: A curve is given parametrically and a first or second derivative is required.
type-2.why: Rates with respect to the parameter combine by the chain rule.
type-2.mistake: Treating the ratio of second parameter derivatives as the second derivative.
type-2.hint: Find the first derivative as a ratio before differentiating again.

type-3.when: A stationary point of a parametric curve must be located and classified.
type-3.why: The first derivative vanishes at a regular stationary point and the second derivative tests its local shape.
type-3.mistake: Accepting a parameter value without checking the denominator of the first derivative.
type-3.hint: Solve for a zero first derivative and check the curve is regular there.

type-4.when: A derivative contains hyperbolic or inverse functions.
type-4.why: The standard derivative is combined with the chain or product rule.
type-4.hint: Identify the outer function and the inner expression separately.

type-5.when: A Maclaurin polynomial is needed to a stated order.
type-5.why: Derivatives at zero determine the polynomial coefficients.
type-5.mistake: Omitting factorials or calculating more orders than requested.
type-5.hint: List the required derivatives at zero or start from a known series.

type-1.when: A square root matches a trigonometric or hyperbolic identity.
type-1.why: The substitution converts the root into an expression that simplifies with the differential.
type-1.mistake: Changing the variable without changing the differential or limits.
type-1.hint: Match the sign inside the square root to a standard identity.

type-2.when: The integrand resembles an inverse-function derivative.
type-2.why: Completing the square puts the denominator into a standard integral form.
type-2.mistake: Losing a scale factor after completing the square.
type-2.hint: Complete the square before choosing the standard integral.

type-3.when: The integrand is a product and one factor simplifies on differentiation.
type-3.why: The product rule rearranges into the integration-by-parts formula.
type-3.mistake: Omitting the boundary term in a definite integral.
type-3.hint: Choose the factor that becomes simpler as the differentiated factor.

type-4.when: An integral is indexed by a power and a recurrence is requested.
type-4.why: Integration by parts relates the indexed integral to a lower power.
type-4.mistake: Leaving the repeated integral on both sides without collecting it.
type-4.hint: Split off a factor suitable for integration by parts.

type-5.when: The length of a curve is requested in Cartesian, parametric or polar form.
type-5.why: The arc-length element combines the horizontal and vertical rates along the curve.
type-5.mistake: Using a formula for a different coordinate form.
type-5.hint: Identify the coordinate form before choosing the length formula.

type-6.when: A curve rotates around a specified axis.
type-6.why: A short arc generates a thin band with circumference determined by its distance from the axis.
type-6.mistake: Using the wrong coordinate as the radius.
type-6.hint: Mark the rotation axis and the perpendicular distance to it.

type-7.when: A positive decreasing series is compared with an integral.
type-7.why: Rectangles lie above or below the curve and bound the sum.
type-7.mistake: Reversing the inequality or shifting the limits incorrectly.
type-7.hint: Sketch the first rectangle and the corresponding interval.

type-1.why: De Moivre’s theorem and binomial expansion express the same complex power.
type-1.mistake: Mixing up real and imaginary coefficients.
type-1.hint: Expand the complex power and group its real and imaginary parts.

type-2.when: A polynomial matches a multiple-angle relation after substitution.
type-2.why: The identity turns algebraic roots into angles with known trigonometric values.
type-2.mistake: Listing repeated roots or missing the required angle interval.
type-2.hint: Match the coefficients to the appropriate trigonometric identity.

type-3.when: A power of sine or cosine needs rewriting before integration.
type-3.why: Opposite powers of the complex exponential combine into multiple-angle terms.
type-3.mistake: Dropping a factor when converting exponentials back to trigonometric terms.
type-3.hint: Write sine or cosine in terms of a complex exponential and its reciprocal.

type-4.when: All complex roots of a power equation are required.
type-4.why: Adding complete turns before dividing the argument gives all distinct roots.
type-4.mistake: Dividing only the principal argument and finding just one root.
type-4.hint: Include the integer multiple of a full turn before dividing the argument.

type-5.when: A finite sine or cosine sum has a geometric pattern.
type-5.why: Real and imaginary parts of one complex geometric sum give the two trigonometric sums.
type-5.mistake: Taking the real or imaginary part before simplifying the complex fraction.
type-5.hint: Write one complex series with the required ratio.

type-1.when: A probability density is given and the cumulative distribution is required.
type-1.why: Integrating density from the support boundary accumulates probability.
type-1.mistake: Restarting the cumulative probability at zero on each interval.
type-1.hint: Find the support and carry the accumulated probability into each new interval.

type-2.when: A probability between bounds or a percentile is required.
type-2.why: A CDF measures probability to the left of a value.
type-2.mistake: Using the tail probability itself as the CDF target.
type-2.hint: Translate the probability statement into a CDF equation first.

type-3.when: An expectation, transformed expectation or variance is required.
type-3.why: Weighting each value by its density gives a moment; variance then uses the first two moments.
type-3.mistake: Using a CDF as though it were the density.
type-3.hint: If the question gives a CDF, differentiate it before calculating moments.

type-4.when: A new random variable is defined as a function of the original one.
type-4.why: Expressing its cumulative event in the original variable gives the new distribution.
type-4.mistake: Failing to reverse the inequality for a decreasing transformation.
type-4.hint: Determine the transformed support and whether the transformation increases or decreases.

type-1.when: One normal-population mean is tested with unknown variance.
type-1.why: Estimating the variance gives the t statistic with one fewer degree of freedom than the sample size.
type-1.mistake: Using the population-variance divisor for the unbiased sample variance.
type-1.hint: State the hypotheses and calculate the unbiased sample variance.

type-2.when: Two large independent samples are used to compare means.
type-2.why: The variance of a difference of independent means is the sum of their variances.
type-2.mistake: Subtracting the estimated variances instead of adding them.
type-2.hint: Fix the direction of the difference before writing the alternative hypothesis.

type-3.when: Two small independent normal samples have equal unknown variances.
type-3.why: Pooling combines their within-sample information into one variance estimate.
type-3.mistake: Using the pooled test without the equal-variance assumption.
type-3.hint: State the assumptions and calculate the pooled variance.

type-4.why: Taking differences removes the pairing and leaves a one-sample test on those differences.
type-4.mistake: Treating paired observations as independent samples.
type-4.hint: Choose a consistent direction for every paired difference.

type-5.when: A confidence interval for one normal mean has unknown variance.
type-5.why: The t multiplier accounts for estimating the population variance.
type-5.mistake: Using a one-tail probability as the two-sided confidence multiplier.
type-5.hint: Find the confidence level and the correct degrees of freedom.

type-6.when: An interval estimates the difference between two population means.
type-6.why: The same difference direction and its standard error determine both interval endpoints.
type-6.mistake: Changing the order of subtraction halfway through the calculation.
type-6.hint: State the difference direction and decide which standard error is justified.

type-7.when: An existing interval is changed to a new confidence level.
type-7.why: The centre and standard error stay fixed while the critical multiplier changes.
type-7.mistake: Changing the centre along with the confidence level.
type-7.hint: Recover the midpoint and half-width of the original interval.

type-1.when: Observed category counts are compared with a discrete uniform model.
type-1.why: Equal model probabilities give equal expected frequencies.
type-1.mistake: Pooling categories after calculating separate contributions instead of pooling counts first.
type-1.hint: Calculate the expected count in every category.

type-2.when: Counts are compared with a binomial distribution.
type-2.why: Model probabilities multiplied by the sample size give expected frequencies.
type-2.mistake: Forgetting the extra lost degree of freedom when the success probability is estimated.
type-2.hint: Decide whether the success probability is given or estimated.

type-3.when: Counts are compared with a Poisson distribution.
type-3.why: Poisson probabilities determine the expected counts, including the tail.
type-3.hint: Find the model mean and include all probability beyond the last listed value.

type-4.when: Grouped continuous data are compared with a normal distribution.
type-4.why: Normal interval probabilities give expected frequencies for each class.
type-4.mistake: Using class midpoints in place of class-boundary probabilities.
type-4.hint: Write the class boundaries and account for both tails.

type-5.when: Grouped counts are compared with a continuous uniform model.
type-5.why: A class probability is its width divided by the full support width.
type-5.mistake: Giving unequal-width classes equal expected frequencies.
type-5.hint: Calculate every class width within the model support.

type-6.when: A specified density is tested against grouped data.
type-6.why: Integrating the density over a class gives its model probability.
type-6.mistake: Estimating a parameter that the question already specifies.
type-6.hint: Integrate over each class before multiplying by the sample size.

type-7.when: A contingency table is used to test association.
type-7.why: Independence makes each expected count the product of its marginal proportions and the total.
type-7.mistake: Using the number of cells for the degrees of freedom.
type-7.hint: Calculate the row totals, column totals and grand total first.

type-1.when: A population median is tested without a normal model.
type-1.why: Under the null median, a non-tied observation is equally likely to lie above or below it.
type-1.mistake: Including observations equal to the hypothesised median in the effective sample size.
type-1.hint: Count positive and negative deviations, setting aside zero deviations.

type-2.when: A median/location test can assume continuous symmetric deviations.
type-2.why: Signed ranks use both the direction and relative size of deviations.
type-2.mistake: Ranking signed values instead of their absolute values.
type-2.hint: Find absolute deviations, rank them, then restore the signs.

type-3.when: A sufficiently large signed-rank sum is approximated by a normal distribution.
type-3.why: Under the stated no-tie conditions the rank sum has a known mean and variance.
type-3.mistake: Applying the continuity correction in the wrong direction.
type-3.hint: Write the discrete tail event before applying a continuity correction.

type-4.when: A paired comparison needs a sign test.
type-4.why: One difference per pair tests the median change using its sign.
type-4.mistake: Counting the signs of original observations rather than paired differences.
type-4.hint: Form the differences in one consistent direction.

type-5.when: Matched-pair differences are continuous and symmetric.
type-5.why: Signed ranks test the location of the paired differences using their magnitudes and signs.
type-5.mistake: Using an independent-samples rank test for matched pairs.
type-5.hint: Form paired differences before ranking their absolute values.

type-1.when: A nonnegative integer-valued distribution is given in a table.
type-1.why: The power records the value and the coefficient records its probability.
type-1.mistake: Using the probability as the exponent.
type-1.hint: Write one term for each possible value and check the coefficients add to one.

type-2.when: A standard discrete distribution is identified.
type-2.why: Its probability terms sum to the corresponding closed-form PGF.
type-2.mistake: Using a geometric PGF with the wrong starting value.
type-2.hint: Check the support as well as the distribution name.

type-3.when: Mean and variance are required from a PGF.
type-3.why: The derivatives at one give the first moment and the second factorial moment.
type-3.mistake: Treating the second derivative as the ordinary second moment.
type-3.hint: Differentiate before substituting the value one.

type-4.when: A game stops on a random numbered attempt.
type-4.why: The stopping probabilities often form separate geometric series for odd and even attempts.
type-4.mistake: Missing a possible stopping outcome or double-counting an attempt.
type-4.hint: Write the first few stopping probabilities before summing.

type-5.when: A sum contains independent integer-valued random variables.
type-5.why: Independence lets the product of the individual powers separate inside the expectation.
type-5.hint: Check independence, then write one PGF for each summand.

type-6.when: A random variable is changed by a fixed scale and shift.
type-6.why: The exponent separates into a shifted power and a substituted original PGF.
type-6.mistake: Replacing the PGF argument by a linear expression instead of a power.
type-6.hint: Write the new variable in the exponent before taking the expectation.

type-1.when: Calculate a moment or balance moments.
type-1.hint: Multiply each force by its perpendicular distance from the pivot. Choose one turning direction as positive. In equilibrium, clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance.

type-2.when: Find the centre of mass of particles or a framework.
type-2.hint: Choose an origin. Form a separate mass-times-distance equation for each coordinate, then divide by the total mass.

type-3.when: Find the centre of mass of a lamina by integration.
type-3.hint: Use a thin vertical strip. Its mass is proportional to its area and its centre is halfway up the strip.

type-4.when: Find the centre of mass of a circular sector.
type-4.hint: Use the total sector angle 2α in radians. The centre lies on the angle bisector. Use the area formula for a lamina and the arc formula for a wire.

type-5.when: Find the centre of mass after removing an area.
type-5.hint: For a uniform lamina, use areas as masses. Give every removed part a negative area and subtract its moments as well.

type-6.when: Find the centre of mass of a composite wire.
type-6.hint: Use mass per unit length times length for each piece. A semicircular arc has its centre of mass on the symmetry axis, a distance 2r/π from the circle centre.

type-7.when: Find the centre of mass of a composite solid.
type-7.hint: Use density times volume. For a removed solid, subtract its mass and its moment. Measure all distances from the same reference plane.

type-8.when: Find the angle when a body is freely suspended.
type-8.hint: Find the combined centre of mass first. When suspended from A, the line AG is vertical. Use the right triangle joining A, G and the symmetry axis.

type-9.when: Find the angle at which a body topples.
type-9.hint: At the toppling limit, the vertical line through the centre of mass passes through the downhill edge. Use the right triangle from that edge to the centre of mass.

type-10.when: Solve a ladder problem with limiting friction.
type-10.hint: Draw all forces. A smooth wall gives only a normal reaction. Resolve horizontally and vertically, then take moments about the foot. Use limiting friction at limiting equilibrium.

type-11.when: Solve equilibrium of a rod supported by a string.
type-11.hint: Draw the tension along the string and the normal reaction perpendicular to the wall. Take moments about the contact point to find the tension, then resolve forces to find friction and the normal reaction.

type-12.when: Decide whether a body slides or topples.
type-12.hint: Find the friction limit and the toppling limit separately. At toppling, the normal reaction acts through the edge. Compare the applied force with both limits.
